claim: SARS-CoV-2 non-structural protein 1 (Nsp1) contains an N-terminal domain and C-terminal helices connected by a short linker region.
source: The SARS-CoV-2 non-structural protein 1 (Nsp1) contains an N-terminal domain and C-terminal helices connected by a short linker region.
evidence: This is supported by structural data referenced in the manuscript and shown in figures.

claim: The C-terminal helices of Nsp1 (Nsp1-C-ter) from SARS-CoV-2 bind in the mRNA entry channel of the 40S ribosomal subunit.
source: The C-terminal helices of Nsp1 (Nsp1-C-ter) from SARS-CoV-2 bind in the mRNA entry channel of the 40S ribosomal subunit and blocks mRNA entry, thereby shutting down host protein synthesis.
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM structural studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: Nsp1-C-ter blocks mRNA entry into the ribosome, thereby shutting down host protein synthesis.
source: The C-terminal helices of Nsp1 (Nsp1-C-ter) from SARS-CoV-2 bind in the mRNA entry channel of the 40S ribosomal subunit and blocks mRNA entry, thereby shutting down host protein synthesis.
evidence: This mechanism is supported by structural and functional studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: Nsp1 suppresses host immune function.
source: Nsp1 suppresses host immune function and is vital for viral replication.
evidence: This is supported by references to studies showing Nsp1's role in immune suppression.

claim: Nsp1 is vital for viral replication.
source: Nsp1 suppresses host immune function and is vital for viral replication.
evidence: This is supported by the literature on SARS-CoV-2 biology.

claim: Montelukast sodium hydrate binds to Nsp1 with a binding affinity (KD) of 10.8 ± 0.2 µM in vitro.
source: Among the top hits obtained, montelukast sodium hydrate binds to Nsp1 with a binding affinity (KD) of 10.8 ± 0.2 µM in vitro.
evidence: This is directly measured using bio-layer interferometry experiments shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Montelukast sodium hydrate forms a stable complex with Nsp1-C-ter in simulation runs with –95.8 ± 13.3 kJ/mol binding energy.
source: It forms a stable complex with Nsp1-C-ter in simulation runs with –95.8 ± 13.3 kJ/mol binding energy.
evidence: This is calculated from molecular dynamics simulations described in the methods and results.

claim: Montelukast sodium hydrate rescues the inhibitory effect of Nsp1 in host protein synthesis, as demonstrated by the expression of firefly luciferase reporter gene in cells.
source: Montelukast sodium hydrate also rescues the inhibitory effect of Nsp1 in host protein synthesis, as demonstrated by the expression of firefly luciferase reporter gene in cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase assays shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Montelukast sodium hydrate shows antiviral activity against SARS-CoV-2 with reduced viral replication in HEK cells expressing ACE2 and Vero-E6 cells.
source: Importantly, it shows antiviral activity against SARS-CoV-2 with reduced viral replication in HEK cells expressing ACE2 and Vero-E6 cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by viral replication assays shown in Figure 3.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 is an enveloped positive-strand RNA-containing virus and belongs to beta coronavirus family.
source: SARS-CoV-2, the causative agent of severe coronavirus disease-19 (COVID-19) pandemic, is an enveloped positive-strand RNA-containing virus and belongs to beta coronavirus family (V'kovski et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge about SARS-CoV-2 supported by citation.

claim: The SARS-CoV-2 virus contains nearly 30 kb RNA genome with 5'-cap and 3' poly-A tail.
source: The virus contains nearly 30 kb RNA genome with 5'-cap and 3' poly-A tail (Finkel et al., 2021; V'kovski et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge about SARS-CoV-2 genome structure supported by citations.

claim: The SARS-CoV-2 genome encodes for 14 open reading frames (ORFs).
source: The SARS-CoV-2 genome encodes for 14 open reading frames (ORFs).
evidence: This is established knowledge about SARS-CoV-2 genome organization.

claim: Upon entry into host cells, ORF1a and ORF1b encode for two polyproteins, which are later auto-proteolytically cleaved into 16 proteins, namely Nsp1–Nsp16.
source: Upon entry into host cells, ORF1a and ORF1b encode for two polyproteins, which are later auto-proteolytically cleaved into 16 proteins, namely Nsp1–Nsp16.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SARS-CoV-2 protein processing.

claim: Nsp1 binds in the mRNA entry channel of the 40S ribosomal subunit and blocks the entry of mRNAs, thereby shutting down host protein synthesis.
source: Among these proteins, Nsp1 binds in the mRNA entry channel of the 40S ribosomal subunit and blocks the entry of mRNAs, thereby shutting down host protein synthesis.
evidence: This is supported by structural and functional studies.

claim: Nsp1 induces endonucleolytic cleavage of host RNAs.
source: Nsp1 also induces endonucleolytic cleavage of host RNAs.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Nsp1 function.

claim: Cryo-EM structures of ribosomes from Nsp1-transfected human HEK293T cells indicate the binding of Nsp1 with 40S and 80S ribosomal subunits.
source: The cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structures of ribosomes from Nsp1-transfected human HEK293T cells indicate the binding of Nsp1 with 40S and 80S ribosomal subunits (Schubert et al., 2020; Thoms et al., 2020; Tidu et al., 2020; Vankadari et al., 2020; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by cited cryo-EM structural studies and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Nsp1 contains 180 amino acids with N-terminal (1–127 amino acids) and C-terminal (148–180 amino acids) structured regions connected by a loop region of about 20 amino acids.
source: Nsp1 contains 180 amino acids with N-terminal (1–127 amino acids) and C-terminal (148–180 amino acids) structured regions connected by a loop region of about 20 amino acids (Schubert et al., 2020; Thoms et al., 2020; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by structural studies and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The C-terminal region of Nsp1 (Nsp1-C-ter) contains two helices that harbor a conserved positively charged motif (KH-X5-R/Y/Q-X4-R).
source: This C-terminal region of Nsp1 (Nsp1-C-ter) contains two helices that harbors a conserved positively charged motif (KH-X5-R/Y/Q-X4-R).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of Nsp1.

claim: The deposition of positive charge toward one edge of the C-terminal helices enhances their ability to bind helix h18 of 18S rRNA.
source: The deposition of positive charge toward one edge of these helices enhances their ability to bind helix h18 of 18S rRNA.
evidence: This is inferred from structural studies showing the interaction interface.

claim: The other side of C-terminal helices interacts with ribosomal proteins uS3 and uS5 in mRNA entry tunnel of the 40S.
source: The other side of C-terminal helices interacts with ribosomal proteins uS3 and uS5 in mRNA entry tunnel of the 40S (Schubert et al., 2020; Thoms et al., 2020; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, zoomed view).
evidence: This is shown in cryo-EM structures cited and displayed in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: These interactions enable Nsp1-C-ter to bind deep into the mRNA entry tunnel and prevent the binding of mRNAs, thereby inhibiting host protein synthesis.
source: These interactions enable Nsp1-C-ter to bind deep into the mRNA entry tunnel and prevent the binding of mRNAs, thereby inhibiting host protein synthesis (Schubert et al., 2020; Thoms et al., 2020; Tidu et al., 2020).
evidence: This mechanism is supported by structural and functional studies cited.

claim: Nsp1 helps in hijacking the host translational machinery.
source: Thus, Nsp1 helps in hijacking the host translational machinery (Yuan et al., 2020) and renders the cells incapable of mounting an innate immune response to counter the viral infection (Narayanan et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on Nsp1 function.

claim: Nsp1 renders the cells incapable of mounting an innate immune response to counter the viral infection.
source: Thus, Nsp1 helps in hijacking the host translational machinery (Yuan et al., 2020) and renders the cells incapable of mounting an innate immune response to counter the viral infection (Narayanan et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on Nsp1's role in immune suppression.

claim: Mutating the positively charged residues K164 and H165 in Nsp1-C-ter to alanines leads to a decrease in binding affinity of Nsp1 with ribosome and fails to inhibit host protein synthesis.
source: Mutating the positively charged residues K164 and H165 in Nsp1-C-ter to alanines leads to a decrease in binding affinity of Nsp1 with ribosome and fails to inhibit host protein synthesis (Schubert et al., 2020; Thoms et al., 2020; Tidu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by mutagenesis studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: Nsp1 is a highly conserved protein and less than 3% of SARS-CoV-2 genomic sequences analyzed showed mutation in Nsp1.
source: Nsp1 is a highly conserved protein and less than 3% of SARS-CoV-2 genomic sequences analyzed showed mutation in Nsp1 (Min et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis cited in the manuscript.

claim: Nsp1-C-ter showed a much reduced frequency of mutations.
source: Further, Nsp1-C-ter showed a much reduced frequency of mutations (Min et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis cited in the manuscript.

claim: The drugs docked to a small region of Nsp1-C-ter consisting of residues (P153, F157, N160, K164, H165, and R171) which coincides with its ribosome-binding interface.
source: The drugs docked to a small region of Nsp1-C-ter consisting of residues (P153, F157, N160, K164, H165, and R171) which coincides with its ribosome-binding interface (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is shown by molecular docking studies and displayed in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The residues in Nsp1-C-ter involved in binding drugs show minimal mutations in worldwide deposited 4,440,705 sequences of SARS-CoV-2 genome in GISAID database.
source: The residues in Nsp1-C-ter involved in binding drugs show minimal mutations in worldwide deposited 4,440,705 sequences of SARS-CoV-2 genome in GISAID database (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is based on genomic database analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Montelukast is regularly used to make breathing easier in asthma.
source: Montelukast is regularly used to make breathing easier in asthma (Paggiaro and Bacci, 2011), while saquinavir is an anti-retroviral drug used in the treatment of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) (Khan et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Saquinavir is an anti-retroviral drug used in the treatment of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV).
source: Montelukast is regularly used to make breathing easier in asthma (Paggiaro and Bacci, 2011), while saquinavir is an anti-retroviral drug used in the treatment of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) (Khan et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Montelukast and saquinavir show binding to Nsp1 but not with Nsp1∆C.
source: We found that montelukast and saquinavir show binding to Nsp1 (Figure 1A) but not with Nsp1∆C (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by BLI experiments shown in Figure 1A and 1B.

claim: Montelukast and saquinavir bind to Nsp1-C-ter.
source: This indicates that montelukast and saquinavir bind to Nsp1-C-ter.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential binding to Nsp1 vs Nsp1∆C.

claim: Saquinavir shows a binding affinity of 7.5 ± 0.5 µM toward Nsp1-C-ter.
source: Montelukast shows a binding affinity (Kd) of 10.8 ± 0.2 µM (Figure 1C) while saquinavir shows a binding affinity of 7.5 ± 0.5 µM toward Nsp1-C-ter (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is measured by BLI experiments shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Montelukast shifts the ∆Tm by 4.3°C.
source: We observed that montelukast shifts the ∆Tm by 4.3°C while the saquinavir causes a ∆Tm shift by 6.5°C (Figure 1E, F).
evidence: This is measured by NanoDSF experiments shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Saquinavir causes a ∆Tm shift by 6.5°C.
source: We observed that montelukast shifts the ∆Tm by 4.3°C while the saquinavir causes a ∆Tm shift by 6.5°C (Figure 1E, F).
evidence: This is measured by NanoDSF experiments shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Montelukast showed binding to Nsp1-C-ter with a 5.61 docking score.
source: The molecular screening experiment shows the binding of montelukast with Nsp1-C-ter with a 5.61 docking score (Supplementary file 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is calculated from molecular docking studies.

claim: At the end of the simulation run, montelukast shows a stable complex by forming H-bonds with E148 and L149, while F157 and L173 form base stacking interactions.
source: At the end of the simulation run, montelukast shows a stable complex by forming H-bonds with E148 and L149, while F157 and L173 form base stacking interactions (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is shown by molecular dynamics simulation analysis in Figure 1H.

claim: Saquinavir shows binding with Nsp1 with a docking score of 5.6.
source: Saquinavir shows binding with Nsp1 with a docking score of 5.6 (Supplementary file 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is calculated from molecular docking studies.

claim: The residues T151, M174, and R175 form H-bonds with saquinavir while R171 forms base stacking interaction at the end of the run.
source: The residues T151, M174, and R175 form H-bonds with saquinavir while R171 forms base stacking interaction at the end of the run (Figure 1J).
evidence: This is shown by molecular dynamics simulation analysis in Figure 1J.

claim: Montelukast and saquinavir bind with Nsp1 with binding energies of –95.8 ± 13.3 kJ/mol and –42.7 ± 5.2 kJ/mol, respectively.
source: Montelukast and saquinavir bind with Nsp1 with binding energies of –95.8 ± 13.3 kJ/mol and –42.7 ± 5.2 kJ/mol, respectively.
evidence: This is calculated using gmx_MMPBSA from molecular dynamics simulations.

claim: Co-transfection of Nsp1 with capped luciferase reporter mRNA causes reduction of luciferase expression.
source: Since Nsp1 is known to inhibit host protein synthesis by blocking the mRNA entry tunnel on the ribosome and co-transfection of Nsp1 with capped luciferase reporter mRNA causes reduction of luciferase expression (Thoms et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on Nsp1 function.

claim: Co-transfection of Nsp1 decreased the luciferase activity by almost half, which is restored by the increasing amount of montelukast.
source: Co-transfection of Nsp1 decreased the luciferase activity by almost half, which is restored by the increasing amount of montelukast (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase reporter assays shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Saquinavir is unable to rescue the Nsp1-mediated translation inhibition.
source: However, we do not observe a similar rescue of luciferase activity in the presence of saquinavir (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase reporter assays shown in Figure 2B.

claim: There was no significant change in gene expression of the firefly luciferase FLuc gene.
source: There was no significant change in gene expression of the firefly luciferase FLuc gene (Figure 2C, D).
evidence: This is shown by qRT-PCR data in Figure 2C and 2D.

claim: Montelukast and saquinavir showed minimal toxicity up to 10 µM in both HEK293T-ACE2 and Vero-E6 cell lines.
source: Results showed minimal toxicity up to 10 µM montelukast and saquinavir in both cell lines.
evidence: This is demonstrated by cytotoxicity assays shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: In Vero-E6 cells, the highest concentration (20 µM) of both drugs showed an almost 80% decrease in cell viability, compared to untreated cell control.
source: However, in Vero-E6 cells, the highest concentration (20 µM) of both drugs showed an almost 80% decrease in cell viability, compared to untreated cell control (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by cytotoxicity assays shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: At a concentration of 10 µM, montelukast showed significant antiviral activity, as indicated by reduced expression of viral spike protein in HEK293T-ACE2 and Vero-E6 cells.
source: At a concentration of 10 µM, montelukast showed significant antiviral activity, as indicated by reduced expression of viral spike protein in HEK293T-ACE2 and Vero-E6 cells (Figure 3A, D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by western blot analysis shown in Figure 3A and 3D.

claim: Montelukast treatment demonstrated up to 1-log reduction in viral copy number in both HEK293T-ACE2 and Vero-E6 cells at 10 µM concentration.
source: The corresponding qRT-PCR data demonstrated up to 1-log reduction in viral copy number in both HEK293T-ACE2 and Vero-E6 cells at this concentration (Figure 3B, E), supported by a decrease in infectious virus titer measured by plaque assay (Figure 3C, F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3B and 3E.

claim: Montelukast treatment resulted in a decrease in infectious virus titer measured by plaque assay.
source: The corresponding qRT-PCR data demonstrated up to 1-log reduction in viral copy number in both HEK293T-ACE2 and Vero-E6 cells at this concentration (Figure 3B, E), supported by a decrease in infectious virus titer measured by plaque assay (Figure 3C, F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by plaque assays shown in Figure 3C and 3F.

claim: No significant antiviral effects were observed in the presence of 10 µM saquinavir.
source: No significant antiviral effects were observed in the presence of 10 µM saquinavir (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by viral replication assays shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Nsp1 is a major virulence factor in SARS-CoV2 which effectively blocks the synthesis of major immune effectors (IFN-β, IFN-λ1, and interleukin-8, retinoic acid–inducible gene I), thereby aiding in establishment of the viral infection.
source: Nsp1 is a major virulence factor in SARS-CoV2 which effectively blocks the synthesis of major immune effectors (IFN-β, IFN-λ1, and interleukin-8, retinoic acid–inducible gene I), thereby aiding in establishment of the viral infection (Thoms et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on Nsp1's role in immune suppression.

claim: Nsp1 serves as a blockage to host mRNA entry by interacting with rRNA helix 18 and ribosomal proteins-uS5 and uS3 near the mRNA entry channel of the 40S ribosomal subunit via its C-terminal helices.
source: It serves as a blockage to host mRNA entry by interacting with rRNA helix 18 and ribosomal proteins-uS5 and uS3 near the mRNA entry channel of the 40S ribosomal subunit via its C-terminal helices (Thoms et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by structural studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: Structural studies on 48S-like preinitiation complex on Cricket paralysis viral internal ribosomal entry site in presence of Nsp1 revealed its ability to lock the head domain of 40S ribosome in a closed conformation.
source: Structural studies on 48S-like preinitiation complex on Cricket paralysis viral internal ribosomal entry site in presence of Nsp1 revealed its ability to lock the head domain of 40S ribosome in a closed conformation.
evidence: This is based on structural studies of Nsp1-ribosome complexes.

claim: Nsp1 competes with eIF3j for uS3 and weakens the binding of the eIF3 to the 40S subunit.
source: In addition, it competes with eIF3j for uS3 and weakens the binding of the eIF3 to the 40S subunit (Yuan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on Nsp1-ribosome interactions.

claim: While the host translation is inhibited by the C-terminal helices of Nsp1, its N-terminal domain enhances translation of viral mRNAs by binding to the 5' UTR.
source: While the host translation is inhibited by the C-terminal helices of Nsp1, its N-terminal domain enhances translation of viral mRNAs by binding to the 5' UTR (Gordon et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on Nsp1 function.

claim: Nsp1 interacts with host mRNA export receptor NXF1-NXT1 heterodimer and aids in retention of cellular mRNAs in the nucleus.
source: Moreover, Nsp1 interacts with host mRNA export receptor NXF1-NXT1 heterodimer and aids in retention of cellular mRNAs in the nucleus (Zhang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on Nsp1's role in mRNA export.

claim: The frequency of mutation accumulation in the N-terminal domain was higher than that of the C-terminal domain.
source: Further, Mou et al., 2021 deciphered the frequency of mutation accumulation in the N-terminal domain was higher than that of the C-terminal domain (Mou et al., 2021).
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis cited in the manuscript.

claim: Montelukast is a leukotriene receptor antagonist.
source: Montelukast is a leukotriene receptor antagonist and repurposing montelukast for tackling cytokine storms in COVID-19 patients has been suggested (Sanghai and Tranmer, 2020) and hospitalized COVID-19 patients that were given montelukast had significantly fewer events of clinical deterioration (Khan et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established pharmacological knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Repurposing montelukast for tackling cytokine storms in COVID-19 patients has been suggested.
source: Montelukast is a leukotriene receptor antagonist and repurposing montelukast for tackling cytokine storms in COVID-19 patients has been suggested (Sanghai and Tranmer, 2020) and hospitalized COVID-19 patients that were given montelukast had significantly fewer events of clinical deterioration (Khan et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by cited clinical studies.

claim: Hospitalized COVID-19 patients that were given montelukast had significantly fewer events of clinical deterioration.
source: Montelukast is a leukotriene receptor antagonist and repurposing montelukast for tackling cytokine storms in COVID-19 patients has been suggested (Sanghai and Tranmer, 2020) and hospitalized COVID-19 patients that were given montelukast had significantly fewer events of clinical deterioration (Khan et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by cited clinical studies.

claim: Montelukast appears as a hit against the SARS-CoV-2 main protease, (Mpro) protease, in computational studies.
source: Montelukast also appears as a hit against the SARS-CoV-2 main protease, (Mpro) protease, in computational studies (Abu-Saleh et al., 2020; Sharma et al., 2021).
evidence: This is based on cited computational studies.

claim: Ma and Wang demonstrated that montelukast gives false positive anti-protease activity as it cannot bind the GST-tagged-Mpro in thermal shift assay and native mass spectrometry experiments.
source: However, Ma and Wang demonstrated that montelukast gives false positive anti-protease activity as it cannot bind the GST-tagged-Mpro in thermal shift assay and native mass spectrometry experiments (Ma and Wang, 2021).
evidence: This is based on cited experimental studies.

claim: Montelukast may not be an inhibitor for Mpro protease.
source: Thus, montelukast may not be an inhibitor for Mpro protease.
evidence: This is inferred from the cited study by Ma and Wang.

claim: Montelukast binds to Nsp1, rescues the Nsp1-mediated translation inhibition and has antiviral activity against SARS-CoV-2.
source: Here, we show that montelukast binds to Nsp1, rescues the Nsp1-mediated translation inhibition and has antiviral activity against SARS-CoV-2.
evidence: This is demonstrated by multiple experiments in the manuscript including BLI, luciferase assays, and viral replication assays.

claim: The rescue of shutdown of host protein synthesis machinery by montelukast seems to contribute toward the antiviral activity of the drug.
source: The rescue of shutdown of host protein synthesis machinery by montelukast seems to contribute toward the antiviral activity of the drug; however, further experiments would be essential to figure out detailed mechanism of its antiviral activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined results of translation rescue and antiviral activity experiments.

claim: The C-terminal region of Nsp1 is a druggable target.
source: Overall, our study identifies C-terminal region of Nsp1 as a druggable target and montelukast as a starting point for designing more potent drug molecules against SARS-CoV-2.
evidence: This is concluded from the successful identification of drugs that bind to Nsp1-C-ter and show antiviral activity.

claim: Montelukast can be used as a starting point for designing more potent drug molecules against SARS-CoV-2.
source: Overall, our study identifies C-terminal region of Nsp1 as a druggable target and montelukast as a starting point for designing more potent drug molecules against SARS-CoV-2.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the demonstrated binding and antiviral activity of montelukast.

claim: The three-dimensional coordinates of C-terminal helices of Nsp1 (Nsp1-C-ter; residue numbers 148–180) were taken from the cryo-EM structure of Nsp1-bound 40S (PDB ID: 6ZOJ).
source: The three-dimensional coordinates of C-terminal helices of Nsp1 (Nsp1-C-ter; residue numbers 148–180) were taken from the cryo-EM structure of Nsp1-bound 40S (PDB ID: 6ZOJ).
evidence: This describes the source of structural data used for computational studies.

claim: The FDA-approved drug library containing 1,645 compounds was subjected to in silico molecular screening.
source: The FDA-approved drug library was used to screen the drugs toward Nsp1-C-ter. The drug library containing 1,645 compounds was subjected to in silico molecular screening.
evidence: This describes the computational screening methodology.

claim: The binding pocket for ligands on Nsp1-C-ter was determined by Computed Atlas of Surface Topography of proteins (CASTp) online server.
source: Subsequently, the binding pocket for ligands on Nsp1-C-ter was determined by Computed Atlas of Surface Topography of proteins (CASTp) online server (Tian et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes the computational method used to identify binding pockets.

claim: T151, P153, D156, F157, Q158, N160, K164, H165, S167, T170, R171, E172, L173, R175, and L177 were found to form the binding pocket on Nsp1-C-ter.
source: The T151, P153, D156, F157, Q158, N160, K164, H165, S167, T170, R171, E172, L173, R175, and L177 were found to form the binding pocket.
evidence: This is determined by computational analysis of the Nsp1-C-ter structure.

claim: The gene construct encoding Nsp1 from SARS-CoV-2 in pCDNA 5–3X-Flag-Nsp1 was amplified and sub-cloned into pET28a with N-terminal His-tag.
source: The gene construct encoding Nsp1 from SARS-CoV-2 in pCDNA 5–3X-Flag-Nsp1 was amplified and sub-cloned into pET28a with N-terminal His-tag (Schubert et al., 2020; Thoms et al., 2020) using appropriate primers (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This describes the molecular cloning methodology.

claim: Montelukast and saquinavir showed high clash scores.
source: Montelukast sodium hydrate (hereafter referred to as montelukast) and saquinavir mesylate (hereafter referred to as saquinavir) showed high clash scores (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on computational analysis of drug-ribosome clashes.

claim: Only montelukast and saquinavir induce a change in the melting temperature of Nsp1.
source: We observed that only montelukast and saquinavir induce a change in the melting temperature of Nsp1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by NanoDSF experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: None of the ligands were able to change the melting temperature of the Nsp1∆C protein.
source: None of the ligands were able to change the melting temperature of the Nsp1∆C protein (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by NanoDSF experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The RMSD of C-terminal helices bound with montelukast shows less deviation from the mean atomic positions.
source: In the simulation runs the root mean square deviation (RMSD) of C-terminal helices bound with montelukast shows less deviation from the mean atomic positions (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is shown by molecular dynamics simulation analysis in Figure 1G.

claim: The RMSD plot of saquinavir bound C-terminal helices shows reduced deviation of the protein atoms during the simulation runs from the mean atomic position.
source: The RMSD plot of saquinavir bound C-terminal helices shows reduced deviation of the protein atoms during the simulation runs from the mean atomic position (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is shown by molecular dynamics simulation analysis in Figure 1I.

claim: The residues involved in binding montelukast and saquinavir show extremely low mutational frequency.
source: Overall, the residues involved in binding montelukast and saquinavir show extremely low mutational frequency.
evidence: This is based on genomic database analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: These drugs-bound complexes show higher average H-bonds throughout different replica simulations.
source: We observed that these drugs-bound complexes show higher average H-bonds throughout different replica simulations (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is shown by molecular dynamics simulation analysis in Figure 1—figure supplement 2E.

claim: Binding of montelukast or saquinavir to Nsp1-C-ter may prevent inhibition of host protein synthesis.
source: We hypothesized that binding of montelukast or saquinavir to Nsp1-C-ter may prevent inhibition of host protein synthesis.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the mechanism of Nsp1 action and drug binding.
